definition: Early Bronze Age sailors on the island of Crete who built colourful painted palaces and traded across the sea before classical Greece.
Bronze Age mainland Greek warrior kingdoms famous for giant stone fortress walls and the carved Lion Gate at Mycenae around 1250 BC.
An independent Ancient Greek city-state, including the walled town and its surrounding farmland, that made its own laws and coins (plural: poleis).
The high, steep walled hilltop at the centre of a Greek city-state where marble temples stood and families sheltered during war.
The sunny open-air marketplace and meeting square in a Greek city-state where farmers traded food and male citizens debated news and laws.
The 24-letter Greek writing system with vowels and consonants, adapted from Phoenician sea traders around 800 BC and named after Alpha and Beta.
The shared name proud Ancient Greeks used for themselves across rival valleys and islands, united by one language, alphabet, and family of gods.
Rule by the people (from Greek demokratia, meaning people-power), invented in Athens around 508 BC so adult male citizens voted directly on laws.
The rocky hillside in Athens where thousands of adult male citizens gathered every few days to listen to speeches and vote by raising hands.
A broken pottery shard scratched with a politician's name by Athenian voters to banish an overly bossy leader from Athens for ten years.
A slotted marble lottery machine in Athens that used falling black and white balls to choose 500 courtroom jurors fairly by chance.
Free foreign-born craftworkers and merchants living permanently in Athens who paid city taxes yet were barred from voting as citizens.
Conquered local farmworkers in Sparta forced to grow crops in the valley so Spartan citizen men could train full-time as soldiers.
Sparta's harsh military training system that took citizen boys from home at age seven to live barefoot and drill in army barracks.
Greece's highest snow-capped mountain, where Ancient Greeks believed Zeus, Hera, Athena, and the other chief Olympian gods ruled above the clouds.
The gleaming white-marble temple built atop the Acropolis of Athens in the 400s BC to honour wise patron warrior goddess Athena.
A sacred shrine, most famously Apollo's mountain temple at Delphi, where priestess Pythia spoke mysterious riddles and advice from the gods.
The peaceful agreement (Ekecheiria) announced before every Ancient Olympic Games from 776 BC so warring city-states paused fighting for safe travel.
The prized crown woven from sacred wild-olive branches placed on the head of each victorious athlete at Ancient Olympia.
A heavily armed Greek citizen-soldier carrying a heavy round bronze-faced shield, crested bronze helmet, shin guards, and a long thrusting spear.
A tight shoulder-to-shoulder battle block of Greek hoplites locking round shields edge-to-edge behind rows of forward-pointing spears.
A fast Ancient Greek wooden warship powered by 170 oarsmen seated on three levels and armed at the waterline with a heavy bronze ram.
A curved open-air stone theatre carved into a sunny Greek hillside, such as Epidaurus, where up to 14,000 spectators watched tragedies and comedies.
From Greek words meaning lover of wisdom: a thinker such as Socrates, Plato, or Aristotle who used questions and observation to search for truth.
The ethical promise linked to physician Hippocrates of Kos, pledging doctors to observe natural symptoms carefully and care honestly for sick patients.
The branch of mathematics studying points, lines, angles, triangles, and shapes, mastered by Greek thinkers such as Pythagoras and Euclid.
The blended culture created after Alexander the Great's conquests mixed Greek language, coins, and learning with Egyptian, Persian, and Asian traditions.
Lasting ideas, words, stone column styles, jury trials, and Olympic traditions handed down from Ancient Greece that still shape modern life today.
